summary: TerraVestige is a 3D globe that answers the question at the heart of the challenge: the same Earth variable can rise in one place and fall in another, so where is it really changing, and is the change real? It follows 14 NASA variables across the atmosphere, ocean, ice and land (1981–2025), colours the planet by the trend of 12 of them, fades out every place where the trend is not statistically significant, and opens a "case file" for any city or point: how fast it is changing, whether that is real (seasonal Mann-Kendall with an autocorrelation correction), whether an independent dataset agrees, and where on Earth the same variable is moving the opposite way. Every number is computed from NASA data fetched live from the source; nothing is simulated or hand-entered.
details:
What it does. Pick a variable, such as surface air temperature, sea ice, snow cover, precipitation or soil wetness, and the globe shows its trend per decade for every grid cell. Red rises and blue falls (water variables use brown and teal, ice and snow use orange and purple). Faded colour means the trend did not pass a significance test after correcting for testing thousands of places at once. Search a city or click anywhere to open a case file with:

- the monthly record, its seasonal anomaly and a trend line with a 95% confidence band;

- four answers: what is changing, where, how much (Sen's slope per decade with its 95% interval), and is it significant;

- every test side by side: seasonal Mann-Kendall (with and without the Hamed-Rao correction), Sen's slope, an OLS regression with its p-value and R², and a Welch t-test of the later against the earlier half;

- a second witness: the same trend computed from Copernicus ERA5, with a badge that shows whether the two datasets agree;

- the opposite twin: the place with the strongest significant trend in the other direction, shown side by side;

- "Has the pace changed?": an exploratory before-and-after rate around the best-fitting break year;

- "How many more years?": when a trend is not significant yet, how much longer the record would need to be to detect it (Weatherhead et al., 1998).

Six guided case tours (Arctic warming, Barents Sea ice, the Antarctic Peninsula pause, Mediterranean drought, the Sahel's rain and the US Southwest's soil moisture) each cite a peer-reviewed paper and set its finding next to the live 1981–2025 result, with an "Agrees" or "Differs" badge. Five of six agree. The Mediterranean differs, and the app explains why: the paper studied the 20th century, and a different period can change the answer. A three-question guide suggests a variable for a student's own town, and a glossary and method panel explain every term.

How it works. A FastAPI backend reads NASA POWER directly: the MERRA-2 monthly Zarr store on the AWS Open Data bucket for the global maps, and the NASA POWER point and regional APIs for case files. For every grid cell it runs a seasonal Mann-Kendall test and Sen's slope, corrects the p-value for month-to-month persistence, and applies Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate control across the map. Case files use the Hamed-Rao autocorrelation-corrected test. The React and three.js frontend draws the trend field on a globe with a GPU shader. Results are cached with their fetch time, which the interface shows; the deployed image fills that cache from the live sources when it is built.

Why it matters. Climate change is not uniform, and a single global average hides that. TerraVestige lets a student, a teacher or a journalist test their own place in a minute, with the same statistics a climate scientist would use, and see honestly when the data cannot tell yet.

Honesty by design. Only real, live data is used, with no synthetic or bundled numbers. When a source fails, the app says so instead of showing fallback data. Non-significant results are shown as such. Limits are stated in the app: reanalysis is not a station record, and a case file is a regional average about 50 km across.

Tools. Python (FastAPI, xarray, zarr, s3fs, NumPy, SciPy, pandas, pymannkendall), TypeScript (React, Vite), three.js and globe.gl, Plotly, Docker, Google Cloud Run.

== SI NOTE ==

The code and documentation were written with assistance from Claude (Anthropic), an SI coding assistant, under the direction and review of the project author. Claude also scripted the screen recording and the cuts of the demo video; the footage is the real app, not generated imagery, and the end card says so. The voice-over is our own recorded voice; a speech-to-text model (Whisper, run locally) was used only to find the takes to cut. Every source file carries an AI disclosure header. The app itself uses no AI at run time: every result comes from rule-based statistics on live NASA data.
